author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

text: What if instead of writing UVM/Coco testbench, we just ask the two different AI implement the RTL, one in SystemVerilog and one in VHDL, creating two separate copies of the same design, then just use formal to proof they are functional equivalent.

author.name: Dan B.
author.headline: Seasoned Electrical/FPGA/ASIC/RTL Engineer with individual & managerial experience

comments.text: I don't think writing it in both Verilog and vhdl and proving they are equivalent, proves anything about the functionality of the design?

replies.text: Agree with Dan B.. Equivalence just proves A and B match each other, not that either implements the spec correctly. Two AI models could misread the same requirement identically and still "pass." To validate functionality you'd need a third reference: formal properties derived independently from the spec, proven against both implementations, not just proving them against each other. The two-implementation trick is still a useful bug-diversity filter, but a match alone isn't correctness.

author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

replies.text: the formal assertions is part of the scaffolding when the AI write the SV and VHDL code. Even bring in the 3rd formal properties, it still doesn't solve what if AI misinterpreted the spec problem. Your formal may be wrong itself.

author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

replies.text: if 2 is not enough, ask the 3rd AI to write a HLS implement too

author.name: Dan B.
author.headline: Seasoned Electrical/FPGA/ASIC/RTL Engineer with individual & managerial experience

replies.text: still not enough. You need something that tests and verifies it. Not that does it again and verifies they are the same. You can have as many copies as you want, all with the same bugs. Would you have 10 engineers do the same design, verify they are the same, prove them equivalent, and assume they are correct? What if the spec has specified the active state of a signal incorrectly? All the engineers followed that and you have 10 designs that are all incorrect.

author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

replies.text:
You are asking a philosophical question, what exactly is a bug?

Say it is a USB spec, you ask AI implement both the host and the device. If the host and device can talk with each other (assuming all numbers are good), it is NOT a bug even thought they both intrepreted the spec the same wrong way. (say a message code table is off by 1). The logical solution is actually update the spec to match what is already implemented.

It actually happened to my old company, we OWN a spec in a niche market, our device can talk to each other, everything works fine, no performance lose, actually I think it is a slightly better db than the spec, so we just update the spec instead.
